items.text: CHANGING STATE BETWEEN LIQUID AND GAS CHANGING STATE BETWEEN LIQUID AND GAS

items.label: text
items.text: Evaporation occurs at any temperature, but boiling only occurs at one temperature – the boiling point of the liquid. Puddles of water disappear quite quickly despite the outside temperature often being below 5°C in the winter in the UK. The water in the puddles certainly does not boil at this temperature; the water evaporates. So water will evaporate at, for example, 5°C but only boil at 100 °C.

items.label: text
items.text: CHANGING STATE BETWEEN SOLID AND GAS: SUBLIMATION

items.label: text
items.text: The process of a gas changing into a solid is given various names. Some people call it 'de-sublimation' or 'deposition' and others just use the word 'sublimation' again.

items.label: text
items.text: There are two different ways this can happen, called boiling and evaporation. BOILING

items.label: text
items.text: Figure 1.6 Boiling to become a gas - and condensing to become a liquid.

items.label: text
items.text: Boiling occurs when a liquid is heated so strongly that the particles are moving fast enough to overcome all the forces of attraction between them. The stronger the forces of attraction between particles, the higher the boiling point of the liquid. This is because more energy is needed to overcome these forces of attraction.

items.label: text
items.text: If a gas is cooled, the particles eventually move slowly enough that forces of attraction between them start to form and hold them together as a liquid. The gas condenses.

items.label: text
items.text: Evaporation is different. In any liquid or gas, the average speed of the particles varies with the temperature. But at each temperature, some particles will be moving faster than the average and others more slowly.

items.label: text
items.text: Some very fast particles at the surface of the liquid will have enough energy to overcome the forces of attraction between the particles - they will break away to form a gas. This is evaporation. You don't see any bubbling; the liquid just slowly disappears if it is open to the air. If the liquid is in a closed container, particles in the gas will also be colliding with particles at the surface of the liquid. If they are moving slowly enough they will be held by the attractive forces and become part of the liquid. In a closed container evaporation and condensation will both be occurring at the same time.

items.label: text
items.text: Figure 1.8 This change of state goes directly from a solid to a gas and from a gas to a solid.

items.label: text
items.text: A small number of substances can change directly from a solid to a gas, or from a gas to a solid, at normal pressure without involving any liquid in the process. The conversion of a solid into a gas is known as sublimation and the reverse process is usually called deposition.
